documents: Published paper: Rodríguez Corcho et al. (2022), Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 23, e2022GC010386 (PDF, 22 pages)

entry.evidence: Likewise, the question of how these slab-lithospheric and deep mantle interactions affect the surface kinematics, slab-dip evolution

sequences.source_document: Published paper: Rodríguez Corcho et al. (2022), G-cubed e2022GC010386

steps.action: Poses the question of how arc mechanical properties, collision style, stress-strain evolution and lithospheric-deep mantle (660 km MTZ) interactions are connected, which prior models ignore.
steps.quote: Likewise, the question of how these slab-lithospheric and deep mantle interactions affect the surface kinematics

steps.action: Takes from other groups' 2D models the expectation that slab-anchoring and folding in the MTZ give punctuated compression or extension in the overriding plate.
steps.quote: slab-anchoring and slab-folding in the 660 km MTZ can result in periodic or punctuated episodes of surface compression or extension

steps.action: Takes from Leng & Gurnis (2015) the proposal that remnant-arc mechanical properties drive crustal flow and decouple the plates.
steps.quote: the remnant arc mechanical properties influence crustal flow and cause the mechanical decoupling of the subducting and overriding plates

steps.action: Designs a one-parameter sweep of buoyancy-driven subduction models, varying only effective remnant-arc thickness from 15 to 35 km, following a global compilation of arc thicknesses.
steps.quote: we keep all parameters constant and systematically increase the effective thickness of the remnant arc from 15 to 35 km

steps.action: Sets the model conditions in Underworld2/UWGeodynamics: a 3,600 x 800 km box, layered isothermal viscosity and density, strain weakening, eclogitization, free-slip boundaries, no imposed velocities, and tracers for kinematics, stress and dissipation.
steps.quote: subduction, mantle flow, arc-continent collision, and lithospheric deformation emerge entirely from buoyancy forces

steps.action: Checks the numerical premise with resolution tests on a 720 x 576 grid (5 km x 1.3 km) against the 10.8 km x 5 km production resolution.
steps.quote: Resolution tests were performed to ensure the dynamics of arc-collision were sufficiently resolved

steps.action: Observes in the model outputs four collision stages and two contrasting styles: arc transference with slab-anchoring and folding, or failed transference with slab break-off.
steps.quote: These contrasting styles of collision are either: (a) arc transference and slab-anchoring plus folding; or (b) failed arc transference and slab break-off

steps.action: Compares styles across the arc-thickness sweep and identifies a threshold at about 3% arc-continent density contrast (effective thickness about 32 km).
steps.quote: A density contrast less than 3% (effective arc thicknesses less than 32 km), results in arc transference and slab-anchoring.

steps.action: Extracts surface kinematics from tracers: subduction velocity fluctuates for less buoyant arcs and decays asymptotically for more buoyant arcs.
steps.quote: we observe a fluctuating trend in the subduction velocity of simulations with less buoyant arcs

steps.action: Correlates in time the peaks in subduction velocity and overriding-plate shortening with slab-folding events at 16.5, 35 and 43 Myr.
steps.quote: show punctuated events of increased surface shortening in the continental plate at 16.5, 35, and 43 Myr when episodes of slab-folding occur

steps.action: Runs a no-arc control simulation: it reproduces the fluctuating kinematics but no surface extension, attributing extension to the arc.
steps.quote: Our simulation without an arc displays the same fluctuating pattern observed in the surface kinematics of less buoyant arcs

steps.action: Measures shallow (80 km) and deep (300 km) slab dip through time, finding that the arc steepens then flattens the shallow dip and that folding drives the deep dip to about 90°.
steps.quote: We measured the slab dip at 80 and 300 km depth

steps.action: Correlates viscous dissipation (lithosphere and whole domain) with subduction velocity and folding events, and interprets folding as a punctuated increase in mechanical coupling.
steps.quote: Results show a correlation between the subduction velocity (Figure 9a) and the viscous dissipation

steps.action: Describes strain-rate and stress evolution: a fluctuating compression-extension regime for less buoyant arcs and lithospheric extension for more buoyant arcs during gravitational spreading.
steps.quote: simulations with more buoyant arcs result in lithospheric extension in the continental plate

steps.action: Runs sensitivity tests on arc and overriding-plate strength, model length, initial arc position, upper-lower mantle density and viscosity contrasts, and box depth (1,400 km); the patterns persist.
steps.quote: occur regardless of the density and viscosity contrast between the upper and lower mantle and the height of the model box

steps.action: Compares the two collision styles with accretion modes in the petrological models of Vogt & Gerya (2014) and Dymkova et al. (2016) and finds agreement.
steps.quote: The styles of collision observed in our numerical simulations are in agreement with the modes of accretion described by the 2D petrological models

steps.action: Proposes that arc body forces, released as the orogen's gravitational potential energy dissipates, drive overriding-plate extension and reduce mechanical coupling.
steps.quote: applies a body force (arc body force) directed from the deformed arc to the surrounding oceanic and continental plates

steps.action: Excludes trench kinematics and slab roll-back as drivers of overriding-plate thinning in these models, using the no-arc control that shows no thinning.
steps.quote: these mechanisms are unable to drive lithospheric thinning in the continental plate in the absence of a colliding arc

steps.action: Explains the absence of the arc-free extension seen in Capitanio et al. (2010) and Boutoux et al. (2021) by an auxiliary choice, the strong overriding plate, rather than revising the claim.
steps.quote: We attribute this discrepancy to the strong overriding plate we included in our models

steps.action: Relates the model mechanism to natural cases documented elsewhere (Central Andes, Zagros, closure of the Neo-Tethys).
steps.quote: An example of this is the closure of the Neo-Tethys ocean basin

steps.action: Keeps the claims: arc buoyancy sets the collision style at a 3% density-contrast threshold; arc body forces drive extension; slab-folding increases coupling and compression.
steps.quote: Our simulations show that the buoyancy of intra-oceanic arcs promote lithospheric flow

tree.answer: Yes: arc-continent collision styles and stress evolution, known from active and ancient orogens
No: deep-mantle interactions and stress history are not directly observable; studied by forward simulation
Mechanism: how arc buoyancy and rheology and MTZ interactions control collision style and stress
Partly: arc body forces versus trench kinematics or slab roll-back as drivers of extension
Partly: the no-arc control separates the arc effect from slab-folding effects
Set: numerical conditions, arc thickness swept 15–35 km
Yes, within the model: resolution, strength, geometry and mantle-contrast sensitivity tests
Kept: two styles separated by a 3% density-contrast threshold; mechanism as best explanation
Not shown: no review file supplied

end.claim: Across buoyancy-driven 2D simulations with effective arc thickness 15–35 km, an arc-continent density contrast below about 3% gives arc transference with slab-anchoring and folding, and above about 3% gives failed transference with slab break-off.

decisive_move.sentence: The one-parameter sweep of effective arc thickness (15–35 km), with all else fixed, is what reveals the two styles and the 3% density-contrast threshold.

gates.evidence: Action: a question, not a stated hypothesis, directed the sweep of arc thickness (p. 2, 7). Claim: the no-arc control (p. 12) and the sensitivity tests (p. 17) could have shown the arc effect or the patterns to be artifacts; the 3% threshold itself is read off the sweep, not predicted. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the runs.

imports.item: Stokes flow equations balancing buoyancy, viscous stress and pressure
Drucker-Prager yield criterion with strain weakening
Viscous dissipation from second invariants of strain-rate and stress tensors

novelty_claims.quote: new point of view where lithospheric flow, driven by the arc buoyancy and rheology, controls the post-collisional evolution of arc-continent collision
provide a new mechanism that explains surface and lithospheric extension
we are able to offer a new viewpoint that focuses on how the gravitational spreading of the orogen
provide a new mechanism that causes slab-roll back and explains surface and lithospheric extension in arc-collisional accretionary margins

limits: Composition is none_fits: a numerical parameter sweep with a control run and sensitivity tests. It poses no rival crucial test (not strong_inference), uses no natural traces (not trace_series), and fits the threshold across set runs rather than nature's repetitions. Sub-claims at other statuses: the arc-body-force mechanism for extension and slab-folding as the driver of punctuated compression are best_explanation within the model. Comparison with nature (Andes, Zagros, Neo-Tethys) is qualitative and cited; no field data are tested. The 3% threshold depends on fixed auxiliaries (strong overriding plate, isothermal layered rheology, free-slip top, 2D geometry). The paper itself attributes its mismatch with Capitanio et al. (2010) to the strong overriding plate. The resolution test results sit in the supplement (Figures S6–S8), which was not supplied. The acknowledgments mention two reviewers and editors, but no review file was supplied, so changes made in review are unknown (inference). The sensitivity tests use single parameter values (e.g., 25 km or 15 km arcs), so whether the threshold itself moves under them is not shown.

disagreements.support: The no-arc control shows no lithospheric thinning, so in these models the arc is needed for extension.
disagreements.quote: these mechanisms are unable to drive lithospheric thinning in the continental plate in the absence of a colliding arc

disagreements.target: Capitanio et al. (2010) and Boutoux et al. (2021) models showing overriding-plate extension after slab-folding
disagreements.support: These simulations do not reproduce that arc-free extension; the paper attributes the difference to its strong overriding plate.
disagreements.quote: Our numerical simulations do not display the episodes of surface and lithospheric extension in the overriding plate

alternatives_considered.reason: Cited work shows a free surface does not change stress-regime polarity, only topography, stress magnitude and localization

alternatives_considered.chosen: Strain weakening of the subducting plate's top layer to decouple the plates
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Weak decoupling interface between overriding and subducting plates
alternatives_considered.reason: Not affected by the changes in width and spatial resolution that an interface undergoes during subduction initiation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Isothermal layered parametrization of temperature-dependent viscosity and density
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Thermal gradients and thermal diffusion (thermo-mechanical models)
alternatives_considered.reason: High slab sinking rates make thermal effects insignificant, per cited work

alternatives_considered.chosen: Lower-mantle viscosity 30 times the upper mantle and density contrast 4.3%
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Viscosity contrasts 50, 70, 100; density contrast 2.4%; deeper 1,400 km box
alternatives_considered.reason: Agreement with prior MTZ models and post-glacial rebound constraints

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Resolution of 5 km x 1.3 km (720 x 576 grid)
alternatives_considered.reason: Resolution tests show the coarser grid sufficiently resolves the system

alternatives_considered.chosen: Model length 3,600 km; arc 450 km from the trench
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Model length 7,600 km; arc at 150 km and 850 km

alternatives_considered.chosen: Weak arc (minimum viscosity 1e20 Pa.s) and weak overriding plate
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Stronger arc (1e21 Pa.s), very strong arc (friction 0.6), overriding plate with post-softening friction 0.001 and 0.01
alternatives_considered.reason: Keeps the arc weaker than the continental plate
